editorial:
"Hallelujah!" (1929) is a King Vidor production released by MGM â€” one of the first major Hollywood sound films built around an entirely Black cast. Vidor personally financed a portion of the budget after MGM judged the commercial risk prohibitive, then shot partly on location in Tennessee and Arkansas, a logistical challenge for the era's early sound equipment. Daniel L. Haynes plays Zeke Johnson, a sharecropper whose religious conviction and lust for Nina Mae McKinney's dancer Chick spiral into violence; the screenplay was Vidor's own original conception, not adapted from any prior novel or play. Irving Berlin contributed songs including "Waiting at the End of the Road," and the film earned Vidor a Best Director nomination at the 1929 Academy Awards before being selected for the National Film Registry in 2008. MGM's copyright on the 1929 release ran a 95-year term that expired January 1, 2025 â€” the print and its synchronized soundtrack are now public domain in the United States.

For a creator, the usable material is the 1929 print and original recorded soundtrack (including the Berlin songs as synchronized to the picture). The one rights trap that actually applies is sourcing: Warner Bros. inherited the MGM library and distributes the title commercially, and a copy derived from a modern remaster may carry independent protection on the restoration expression itself, even though the underlying film is free. The Internet Archive item (identifier hallelujah_1929, uploaded December 2024) is the most accessible route, but its chain of custody is not documented in its metadata. A cautious reuser should confirm their working copy does not trace to a labeled commercial restoration before treating all elements as unencumbered. Trademark and restoration status remain unconfirmed and should be investigated before any commercial release.
faq: Can I use footage from Hallelujah! without a license?

The underlying 1929 print is in the public domain â€” MGM's copyright expired January 1, 2025. The caveat is your source: if you pull footage from a commercial DVD or streaming version derived from a modern restoration, that specific restoration expression may carry its own copyright. Use a source traceable to the public-domain print (such as the Internet Archive item) rather than a labeled commercial remaster, and you avoid that problem.
Are the Irving Berlin songs in Hallelujah! still protected?

Not as used in this film. Berlin's contributions â€” including 'Waiting at the End of the Road' â€” were published as part of the 1929 motion picture. The 95-year US copyright term on those 1929 publications expired January 1, 2025, so the compositions as embedded in this film are public domain. Separately released Berlin recordings or sheet music from other years have their own timelines and must be checked individually.
